extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, and practitioners interested in patent prosecution and IP policy (economists, patent scholars, patent attorneys, USPTO/policy stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of continuation applications at the USPTO, with a focus on use of continuations to obtain standard-essential patents (SEPs) and the relation between standard publication and late-claiming behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of continuation application
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuation application seeks protection for new claims based on the invention disclosed in a prior 'parent' application, using the parent's priority date to assess novelty and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that continuations allow applicants to add new claims while retaining the parent's priority date; used to delay claim drafting and to tailor claims later. Example: a continuation contains new claims on the invention disclosed in its parent application and benefits from the original priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / written description support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim in a continuation must be supported by the disclosure in its parent; specifically, the parent application must provide enough information for a 'person having ordinary skill in the art' (PHOSITA) to make and use the claimed invention (the 'enablement' requirement: 35 U.S.C. §112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation on late claiming: claims in continuations cannot introduce subject matter not enabled by the original disclosure. Anti-pattern: drafting continuation claims that lack adequate support in the parent risks invalidation for lack of enablement/written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory patent term limitation for continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuations have a shorter useful life, based on the statutory patent term of 20 years from the parent's priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing continuations preserves the parent's priority date but cannot extend the 20-year term measured from that priority date; strategic tradeoff when deciding to file long chains of continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/window to file continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can file a continuation at any time during the pendency of a parent application or during the pendency of that parent's previous children; chains of continuations can be used to seek new claims many years after the original disclosure (subject to the parent's priority/term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows very long lags between priority date and claim drafting (e.g., 99th percentile lag up to 15 years for certain filings). Important for assessing 'late claiming' relative to observable events (e.g., standard publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of filing continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each continuation costs roughly $6,500 to prosecute; attorney fees commonly range from $3,000 to $6,000 and USPTO fees about $2,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost is a practical limitation and factor in applicants' strategic choices to file continuations or abandon low-value claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions/legitimate uses of continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuations are used to delay claim drafting to better understand the invention, to abandon low-value claims, to lock-in gains during negotiation with an examiner (allowing some claims to issue while continuing to pursue others), to amend claims in response to changes in patent law, and to draft claims that cover new uses of an invention that emerge after the priority date (if supported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates pro-social and strategic reasons for continuations; evaluators should consider the stated purpose when assessing welfare implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-in-part, divisional, and reissue distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation-in-part (CIP) claims new subject matter not entitled to earlier priority; divisionals respond to restriction requirements; reissuance allows correction and (if within 2 years) enlargement of scope but requires surrender of the original patent and is relatively rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These alternative mechanisms each have distinct priority/subject-matter and procedural consequences and should be treated differently when evaluating prosecution strategy or measuring 'late claiming'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on reissuance enlargement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissuance allows the patent owner to correct mistakes and to enlarge the scope of claims if filed within two years of the original grant date, but requires surrender of the original patent and is relatively rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits practical use of reissue to enlarge claims beyond a narrow window; contrasts with continuations which can be used over longer periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: PHOSITA forecasting / notice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: In principle, a PHOSITA should be able to forecast every claim that emerges from a parent application; in practice, vague or opaque written descriptions make forecasting difficult, causing notice failures (Menell & Meurer, 2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of whether continuations harm notice should consider the technical quality and specificity of the parent disclosure; anti-pattern: relying on overly vague descriptions that hinder PHOSITA forecasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential harms: notice failures, holdup, patent thickets
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuations can create ambiguity about the scope of patent rights (notice failures), contribute to patent thickets that increase costs for entrants, and enable holdup where claims drafted late read on already-commercialized technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social welfare effects or policy responses, weigh these harms against potential benefits (e.g., encouraging early disclosure and higher-value claim drafting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential benefits: encouraging early disclosure and conserving USPTO resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuations provide applicants an option to delay claim drafting, which can encourage early invention disclosure (by allowing early filing) and help the USPTO conserve resources by avoiding examination of low-value claims that can be abandoned later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation should consider whether these benefits outweigh the harms in particular sectors or application clusters (e.g., startups vs. incumbent licensors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of continuations to tailor claims to post-disclosure technology ('late claiming')
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may use continuations to draft claims that cover products and technologies developed after the original invention is disclosed — a practice termed 'late claiming'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical indicators of late claiming include filing of continuations after an observable industry milestone (e.g., SSO standard publication) and increased textual similarity of continuation claims to later-published technology. Anti-pattern: drafting claims explicitly to cover known competitor products without adequate original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSO disclosure obligations and FRAND commitments as linking mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Several Standard Setting Organizations (SSOs) require participants to disclose patents that might be infringed by a proposed standard, and commonly require licensing on fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSO disclosures provide an observable link between patent applications and potentially infringing technology; however, assessors should account for mis-measurement due to over-declaration, non-assessment of essentiality by SSOs, blanket disclosures, and non-participation by some owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard publication as observable milestone for evaluating late claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal publication of a standard is used as an observable proxy for the date when uncertainty about product design is resolved, and thus marks when applicants have incentives to tailor claims via continuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of late claiming should compare continuation filing rates before and after standard publication (difference-in-differences, matched controls, etc.). Note that draft circulation and meetings may resolve some uncertainty before formal publication; consider pre-publication windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical identification: matching on filing-quarter, art-unit, and examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate the impact of standard publication on continuation filing, construct controls by matching non-SEP applications on filing quarter, art-unit and examiner (and, where appropriate, pre-standard continuation counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach aims to address selection bias because SEPs are concentrated in ICT fields and selected for ex ante quality. Use DID regressions and robustness checks (placebos, alternative estimators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory double patenting rejection as an examination signal
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-statutory double patenting rejection issued by an examiner signals that applicants are seeking to expand the scope of claims in a parent application (and may indicate strategic late claiming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examination outcome datasets (Office Action Research Dataset) to detect such rejections as empirical evidence of scope-expanding continuation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner leniency as a moderating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of standard publication on continuation filings is larger when patent examiners are more lenient (i.e., when examiners are more likely to allow broader claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or modeling continuation behavior, control for examiner-specific tendencies as they influence issuance probabilities and applicants' strategic incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional and PCT as alternative delay mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional patent application establishes priority and provides up to one year to file a non-provisional with specific claims; PCT international applications allow applicants to amend claims for up to ~30 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These alternatives provide shorter delay windows than continuations but are relevant when assessing an applicant's overall strategy for delaying claim drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement caveats for linking SEPs to standards
rubrics_metrics.description: SSO disclosures do not perfectly identify essential patents: some disclosed patents are non-essential, some essential patents are undisclosed, firms may over-declare to avoid unenforceability, and some SSOs permit blanket disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses using SSO disclosures should acknowledge mismeasurement and incorporate robustness checks; interpret SEP-linked continuation increases in light of these disclosure incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation association as suggestive evidence of effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation filings (especially post-standard continuations) are positively correlated with involvement in U.S. district court litigation among SEPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts ultimately determine infringement, higher litigation incidence is suggestive that some late-claimed continuations target enforceable subject matter; use litigation datasets (e.g., Lex Machina) as part of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual similarity/convergence of claims after standard publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of SEPs become more similar after standard publication; pairwise textual similarity of continuation claims vs parent claims increases following standard publication, consistent with tailoring claims to published standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual similarity metrics can be used as an evaluative measure of late claiming targeted at standards; compare post-standard continuations with pre-standard parents.
